newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar surges to 120 yen only to dive back again.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges to 120 yen only to dive back again.

text.p: The dollar rocketed to 120 yen in Tokyo trading on Friday, its highest level in almost four years, but dived back down as top government officials sent out a slew of seemingly contradictory signals.

Brokers said the dollar hit 120 yen, its highest point since February 1993, after an official at the Bank of Japan said that the weak yen and the recent sharp fall in the stock market would not stall the nation's economic recovery.
"We do not see it (the weakness of the yen and a drop in stock prices) as stalling the economy," Masayuki Matsushima, director of the research department at Japan's central bank, told reporters.
He said that for now the weakness in the yen was working to help boost Japanese corporate profits by making Japanese exports more competitive.

The comments signalled an apparent shifting of gears by Japan's finance mandarins, who have been bemoaning the currency's steep decline since the start of the year. They were taken by the market as signalling that Japan might not stand in the way of a stronger dollar.
His comments were echoed by Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya, who said the recent weakness of the yen was having no major negative impact on Japan's economy.
But then a Ministry of Finance official said the government did not want to see an excessively weak yen and the currency reversed direction.
"Like an excessive appreciation...an excessive depreciation of the yen is not welcome," said the official, who spoke on condition he not be identified.
Adding to the mix, Japan's chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference he was confident the yen would not fall below the 120 yen level against the dollar.
The yen then recovered all of its losses, climbing back to 118.80 to the dollar in late trading. In late U.S. trading on Thursday the dollar had stood at around 119.22 yen.
Also roiling the markets was a report on NHK television that the Bank of Japan had intervened in the currency market to stop the dollar's upward march.
Traders were divided on the issue, however, with most saying they could detect no clear evidence of yen-buying.
The man dubbed "Mr Yen", director-general of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau Eisuke Sakakibara, refused to comment on the subject of intervention.
He was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying that sharp moves in either direction were not desirable.

The yen has tumbled some 50 percent since hitting a postwar high of 79.75 yen to the dollar in the spring of 1995. At that time the Japanese government successfully talked the currency back down, but has since been unable to stop its slide.

The yen's slide has been speeded by a long period of low interest rates, kept low to help the economy recover. This has made the yen an unattractive investment vehicle compared with some other major currencies.
The yen's fall has been mirrored by a sharp fall in Tokyo shares, even though many corporations would benefit from a lower yen, which makes exports more competitive.

Traders say both markets are being hit by overall gloom about the prospects for the Japanese economy despite signs of a recovery after years of stagnation following the bursting of the 1980s asset "bubble".
